Weddings

Elopements, micro weddings and everything in between

The word wedding covers a two person ceremony on a headland and a 180 guest sit down in a ballroom. Different planners, different lead times, different help. Work out your shape first.

Why the shape of a wedding matters more than the size of it

An elopement planner and a planner running a 180 guest reception are solving different problems, not the same problem at different scales. The large wedding is a supplier management job: twelve contracts, a bump in window, a seating chart and one run sheet. The elopement is a permissions job: a celebrant, a legal notice, a place you are allowed to stand, two witnesses and a photographer who can find you.

Shape also decides where the difficulty sits. In a backyard wedding it is infrastructure. In a regional wedding it is guest logistics, because everyone has to sleep somewhere. So describe the shape of your day when you enquire, not just the guest number.

The shapes

Which kind of wedding are you actually having?

Six shapes cover most Australian weddings. The guest counts overlap; the planning does not.

Wedding shapes compared on size, lead time and what the planning help is for.
ShapeGuestsUsual lead timeWhat the planning help is mostly for
ElopementTwo, plus two witnessesFour weeks to four monthsLegal requirements, permissions, location and the right rock at the right hour

Elopements

What does an elopement planner actually arrange in Australia?

More than people expect, and most of it is invisible on the day.

An elopement planner arranges six things: the celebrant, the legal paperwork, permission to be where you want to be, witnesses, the photographer, and the travel around all of it. Styling and florals sit on top, and are the smallest part of the job.

The legal piece is fixed, which is why spontaneous elopements are rarer than films suggest. Australian marriage law requires a Notice of Intended Marriage to be lodged with your authorised celebrant at least one month and one day before the ceremony, and it stays valid for eighteen months. You also need two witnesses aged eighteen or over.

Permission is the piece that catches people. A beach, a headland or a national park is not automatically available because it is public. Many require a booking, a permit or a fee, some cap numbers, and some restrict chairs, arbours, confetti and vehicles. Knowing which sites allow what is the most useful thing an elopement planner carries.

Then there is the part nobody plans for: getting four people, one carrying a camera, to a spot forty minutes' walk from a car park, at the right hour, with a weather fallback.

Lodge the notice early

The Notice of Intended Marriage has to reach your celebrant at least one month and one day before the ceremony. It is the one date that cannot move, so book the celebrant before the location.

Ask what the permit covers

Permits often specify a headcount, a time window and whether you may bring chairs, an arbour or a vehicle. Get the conditions in writing.

Small weddings

Why a small wedding is not proportionally cheaper to plan

Halving the guest list does not halve the work, and what does not shrink is what a planner charges for.

A 40 guest wedding still needs a celebrant, a photographer, a venue, food, drink, music, a cake, flowers and someone to make the day happen in order. That list does not shorten when the guest list does. Only catering and drinks scale cleanly with numbers.

Planning hours behave the same way. Sourcing a photographer takes the same calls whether they shoot 40 people or 140. There is a genuine difference between a wedding planner for small wedding work and a planner whose season is built around large receptions, and it is not that one does less. It is that the specialist knows which venues take small bookings without a punishing minimum spend.

Minimum spends are where small weddings quietly get expensive. A venue wanting $18,000 through the door will happily host 40 people, but you pay for 100 either way. The other trap is standards, because forty guests notice food and wine that a hundred and forty do not.

Away from home

Multi-day weddings and weddings out of town

01

Lock the site before the programme

A regional venue or private property decides what a multi-day wedding can be. Book it first, then design the welcome drinks around it.

02

Solve where guests sleep

In a country town, accommodation is the constraint, not the venue. Hold a block of rooms and name it in the save the date.

03

Plan the movement, not the events alone

Two sites, three days and a bus timetable is a logistics plan. Decide who drives and when the last run leaves.

04

Protect one day for nothing

A three day wedding with every hour programmed exhausts everybody, including you. Leave an unscheduled afternoon in the middle.

Multi-day weddings usually need full planning rather than coordination, because the programme has to be designed before anything can be booked. Our page on wedding planning covers that process, and venue sourcing can be bought alone.

Backyards

Weddings at home or on private property

The cheapest looking option on the list is frequently the most complicated one to run.

Everything is a hire item

A backyard has no kitchen, no bar, no toilets and no shelter. Each arrives on a truck and leaves on one, which means access, a delivery window and a late pack down.

Power is the first phone call

Catering equipment, lighting and a band draw more than a domestic circuit carries. Get the caterer's power requirement in writing before you price a generator.

A wet weather plan is a booking, not an intention

It is a marquee you have booked or a room you have confirmed. A plan that depends on a decision you make on the Thursday is not a plan, and marquee stock vanishes in a wet week.

Neighbours and noise

Council noise rules and a music curfew apply in a residential street even when the party is in a garden. Check what your council allows, and tell the neighbours first.

Getting help

Which planning help suits which shape

Elopements and micro weddings are usually one tightly scoped package. Small and backyard weddings suit partial planning. Full size and multi-day weddings are where full planning earns its fee. See wedding planners, wedding coordinators or the planner cost guide.

Straight answers

Wedding shape questions

What does an elopement planner do?

They arrange the celebrant, hold you to the legal timeline, secure permission for the location, organise witnesses, book the photographer and work out the travel. The valuable part is knowing which beaches, headlands and parks allow a ceremony, and what each permit permits.

How far ahead do I need to plan an elopement in Australia?

The law sets the floor: a Notice of Intended Marriage must reach your authorised celebrant at least one month and one day before the ceremony, and stays valid for eighteen months. Most are planned in four weeks to four months, longer if the location needs a permit.

Is a small wedding cheaper to plan than a large one?

Per guest, usually not. Catering and drinks scale with numbers; the celebrant, photographer, venue hire and planning hours do not. Minimum spends are the sting. Ask whether a planner works as a wedding planner for small wedding formats, because some price a 30 guest day exactly as a 130 guest one.

Do I need a permit to get married on a beach or in a national park?

Frequently yes. Many Australian councils and park authorities require a booking or permit for a ceremony on public land, and some charge a fee, cap numbers or restrict chairs and vehicles. Check before you set the date.

What is the difference between a micro wedding and an elopement?

An elopement is the two of you plus the witnesses the law requires. A micro wedding is a guest list kept deliberately small, usually under 20, with a ceremony and a meal. The legal requirements are identical; a micro wedding adds hosting, seating and a running order.

Can a planner organise a wedding on private property?

Yes, and it is one of the strongest cases for hiring one. A private property wedding means sourcing power, water, toilets, a kitchen, parking and a real wet weather plan on top of the wedding itself. Mention site access and power when you enquire.

One enquiry, then it is somebody else's job
